text: The guide comes to a halt at the edge of the path and asks the walkers to look closely at the flattened grass at their feet. Dew, she tells them, never drops out of the sky, whatever most people on the hills imagine. Through the dark hours the ground gives its warmth away to an open sky, until its surface sits colder than the air resting against it. Moisture in that air then gathers as tiny beads along the chilled blades. One of the walkers objects: yesterday morning she saw nothing of the sort. The wind had been stirring the air all night, the guide answers, so the cooling never took hold. Cloud works the same trick from above, she adds, throwing the warmth back down. And that pale haze lying in the hollow below them? The same business, she says, only spread through a whole layer of air.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: growers of the older generations could do nothing against the rising water

text: You are probably wondering what growers of the older generations could possibly do when the river came up and swelled. They put up with it. The flood tore out the seedlings, drowned the pens, and now and then carried off a whole store hut. Then somebody noticed something odd. Where the water had drawn back, the next harvest came in heavier, and the mud left behind fed the tilled ground better than any dung from the beasts. So the trick was to keep the enrichment and lose the wreckage. The answer arrived by degrees. Channels were dug to lead the flow into shallow basins. Ridges of clay went up along the edges. Gates were cut that a pair of hands could swing open at the chosen moment. In came the water, down went its load, and off it drained. Growing food had stopped being a gamble.

units: two agents shape the stones of a valley in different ways

this distinction makes it possible to rebuild the past of a slope with no clue left
text: Two agents shape the stones of a valley, and they do not go about the work in anything like the same way. A fast stream rolls its boulders along, knocks them one against another and wears them down by steady rubbing; out come pebbles that are round, polished and sorted by size as the course runs on. Ice, for its part, rolls nothing at all. It carries its load like a slow belt and drops it exactly as it was, so the fragments keep their sharp edges and lie jumbled together, a huge block beside a dust of clay. A specialist tells the two deposits apart at a glance. Where water has worked, the grains match one another and settle in clean layers. Where ice has passed, the sediment stays disordered. That difference lets you rebuild the story of a slope on which nothing visible now remains.

units: a child regularly brought back finds picked up in a wood

text: The child would come back from the wood with her pockets weighed down, and nobody could ever guess what she would pull out of them. The feathers came first, laid out by shade, from the darkest to the palest. Then the empty shells, delicate enough to break in her hand. Then strips of bark, which she rubbed and held under her nose for the smell of resin and rain. A squall had brought down a beech in the cold season, and ever since she had been carrying home splinters of pale wood torn from the split trunk. Last of all lay the stones: a streaked pebble, a lump of milky-white quartz, a shard of slate that flaked apart between her fingers. Her elderly grandmother kept none of it herself. She lent a box, listened to the account of every piece, and waited for the following haul.

units: the trial plot must be marked out on an even, uncovered slope

text: Begin by choosing an even slope, clear of any thick cover, and mark out a square plot with wooden pegs. Drive a rigid metal edging into three of the sides, leaving it standing a hand's height above the ground. On the downhill side, fit a sloping gutter that feeds the water into a graduated drum sunk in a pit. Now you wait for a shower to fall. The moment it ends, read off the volume collected, stir the contents well, then draw a sample into a clean bottle. Leave the mud to settle overnight, pour off the clear water, dry the remaining deposit and weigh it. Finally, note down the slope of the plot and the condition of the surface. Repeat after every shower and you will have the solid load carried off by run-off, and you will watch that figure drop as soon as a plant cover takes hold.

text: A crack several paces in length opened up this week along the edge of a farmed plateau, and the authorities have closed the track that crosses it. Survey work carried out by a team of geologists puts the opening down to a run of exceptional showers. Water working downwards through the soil has soaked a clay layer buried beneath the crops; softened in this way, the layer no longer grips what it carries, and the ground above has begun to move towards the slope. Imperceptible at first, the movement quickened once a poorly drained retaining wall gave way. The farmers now fear for the spring that serves their animals, since the crack is diverting part of the underground flow. Measuring instruments will be set in place before the wet season, so that the break can be followed as it widens.

text: Just beyond a low bridge, the river runs up against a spur of rock and swings sharply away to one side. A standing eddy has hollowed itself out at that point, dark at the centre and ringed with brown foam. The inner side of the bend gathers a bank of fine sand, while the outer side gives up about a hand's width every wet season. The alder roots end up hanging in mid-air, and a tree topples over as soon as a rise in the water leaves them bare. The people living along that bank ruled out the pouring of concrete along the edge. What they did instead was drive living willow stakes at an angle into the bank under attack, then weave supple branches between them. The wood takes root, the roots stitch the soil together, and the current loses its force against the drowned foliage.

units: the writer invites us to set two ways of managing a river side by side

text: Honestly, we would do well to set two ways of handling a river side by side before choosing ours. The first shuts it in: the bed is straightened, the banks are hardened, the defences go up another notch at every warning. It works, right up until it does not, and then the water goes off all at once, faster and higher than it ever would have without us. The second way makes less of a show. You give the river back its flood meadows, you pull the buildings away, you accept that fields with nobody living on them will go under. The water spreads, slows, and lays its silt where it feeds instead of ruining. I know the second choice means surrendering land one owns, and surrendering has never pleased anybody. But the first commits us to spending for ever, and its bill lands at the worst possible moment.

text: Nothing whatever marked out a boatman's daughter to become the water scientist whom the keepers of dams now turn to for advice. Her working life falls into three parts. There is the fieldwork first of all: whole seasons spent drawing muddy water from the middle of the current, slung in a cradle above it, to weigh what the river carries away. There is the laboratory next, where she worked out a way of sorting grains so inexpensive that distant teams with no money for equipment took it up. And there is the passing on: every season she takes in beginners and sends them wading in the silt long before she opens a textbook for them. Those close to her describe an abrupt woman, sparing with her praise, yet never able to turn down a call in the middle of the night when a bank threatens to go.

text: The exhibition opens in a room with almost no light, and the reasoning behind it is plain from the doorway, since you listen before you see. A gale turns about the visitor while shadows of cloud slide across the floor. The second room brings out the cases at last: cores of sediment stood up like columns, leaved with pale and dark bands that tell of dry seasons and wet ones. Then comes a more instructive gallery, the weakest stretch by some way, where too many panels repeat what the objects had already said better. The final room makes up for all of it. A wall of damp clay, lit from the side, dries before your eyes and splits open during the visit; the cracking carries through the quiet. You come away having watched matter grow old, something no still image could have conveyed.
